system: You are a helpful assistant. Answer accurately and concisely.
passage: In the spring of 2019, the public library in the small river town of Millbrook began lending something unusual: seeds. The idea came from Rosa Delgado, a retired science teacher who volunteered at the front desk. She noticed that many patrons borrowed gardening books but said that buying seed packets every year was expensive, especially for families on tight budgets. Delgado proposed a simple system. Members could take up to five packets of vegetable, herb or flower seeds each season at no cost. In return, they were encouraged, but not required, to let a few plants go to seed at the end of the summer and bring some of those seeds back to the library. The first year was modest. The library started with about 400 donated packets stored in an old wooden card catalog, and roughly 120 households took part. Many returns were mislabeled or mixed, so volunteers held evening workshops on how to dry, sort and label seeds properly. By 2022, the program had grown to more than 600 participating households and the collection included over 90 varieties, several of them local tomatoes and beans that had been grown in the valley for generations. Not everything went smoothly. Some seeds cross-pollinated and produced plants that looked nothing like the label promised, and the library had to add a warning card explaining which crops are easy to save and which are not. A small group of residents also worried that the program distracted staff from traditional library work. Supporters argue that the benefits are clear. The seed library has brought new visitors through the doors, connected older gardeners with younger ones, and helped preserve plant varieties that might otherwise have disappeared. Other libraries in the region have since visited Millbrook to copy the model.
